> I have generated a vector of service times but i am not being able to
> maintain a global variable to return me the next value of the vector as

If you define something like

consume <- function(x) {
  i <- 0
  function() {
    i <<- i + 1
    x[[i]]
  }
}

Then you can write

trajectorystd <-
  trajectory("Standard path") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", consume(servicetime)) %>%
  seize("STD") %>%
  timeout(function() get_attribute(envs, "start_time")) %>%
  release("STD")

And with the next release, in a few days, you will be able to replace

timeout(function() get_attribute(envs, "start_time"))

with

timeout_from_attribute("start_time")

>
> I have managed to use the set_attribute function to set the delay time but
> is there a more simpler way to do it?

There will be in future releases. Keep an eye on issue #123:

https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/123

Iñaki

>
> Regards,
>
> Salman Memon
>

messages.subject: New release: simmer 3.7.0
messages.subject_clean: New release: simmer 3.7.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A new release of simmer arrived at CRAN this past weekend (see [1])
with several bug fixes and new features, such as the
timeout_from_attribute() activity. Now, instead of

trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("delay", 1) %>%
  # ...
  timeout(function() get_attribute(env, "delay"))

you can write

trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("delay", 1) %>%
  # ...
  timeout_from_attribute("delay")

which is more convenient and faster. Also, setters such as
set_attribute, set_capacity, set_prioritization... include a new
argument called "mod", which allows us to modify the
attribute/capacity/whatever instead of providing a new value. For
example, instead of

trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("delay", 1) %>%
  # ...
  set_attribute("delay", function() get_attribute(env, "delay") + 1)

you can write the much shorter and legible

trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("delay", 1) %>%
  # ...
  set_attribute("delay", 1, mod="+")

Regards,
Iñaki

[1] https://www.enchufa2.es/archives/simmer-3-7-0.html

messages.subject_clean: Timeout of resource seized dependent on an event
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am modelling the flow of fuel to a petrol station. The petrol station is modelled as a resource and is seized for a timeout. I want to model "event A" which happens at a rate of rexp(1,1/100) and once it happens it would cause the timeout of the petrol station to change for a period of time before returning to its original timeout. Is there a way to model this?

I tried using a signal trap handler but the signal sent subscribes to one arrival whereas I need the signal to be subscribed to every arrival that seizes the petrol station for the period of time the signal lasts.

fuel<-trajectory()%>%
  seize("terminal",1)%>%
  log_("Enters terminal ")%>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, 5))%>%
  release("terminal",1)%>%
  log_("Leaves terminal")
  seize("petrol_station",1)%>%
  log_("Enters petrol station")%>%
  set_attribute("petrol arrival time", now(env_value), global=FALSE)%>%
  trap(signal,
     handler= trajectory()%>%
         log_("reduce timeout")%>%
         timeout(5)
  )%>%
  timeout(10)%>%
  release("petrol_station",1)%>%
  log_("Leaves petrol station")

event_A <- trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("signal arrival time", now(env_value), global=FALSE)%>%
  send("event A occured")%>%
  timeout(20) %>%
  log_("event A ends")

env_value%>%
  add_resource("terminal",1)%>%
  add_resource("petrol_station", 1) %>%
  add_generator("fuel_unit", fuel, from(0, function() rexp(1, fuel_interarrival), arrive=TRUE), mon=2)%>%
  add_generator("event_A", event_A, from(0, function() rexp(1,1/200), arrive=TRUE),
                priority = 1, mon=2) %>%
Thanks

S

messages.subject: New feature: add_dataframe
messages.subject_clean: New feature: add_dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm happy to announce a new feature that, judging by the questions
I've been responding lately, will be well-received by many of you. It
aims to meet the need to attach preexistent (or precomputed) data with
attributes.

Until now, this was possible by passing the arrival times to the
add_generator method and then cleverly consuming other attributes
directly in the trajectory (I shared here and on StackOverflow a
function called "consume" for this).

Instead, the new add_dataframe enables the following:

lambda <- 1
mu <- 2

customer_data <- data.frame(
  time    = rexp(1000 * lambda, lambda),
  service = rexp(1000 * mu, mu)
)

customer <- trajectory() %>%
  seize("clerk") %>%
  timeout_from_attribute("service") %>%
  release("clerk")

env <- simmer() %>%
  add_resource("clerk", 1) %>%
  add_dataframe("customer", customer, customer_data) %>%
  run()

which is not only convenient, but very fast. I encourage you all to
try this new feature. It can be tested by installing the feature-data
branch with remotes (or devtools):

remotes::install_github("r-simmer/simmer", ref="feature-data")

Don't forget to read the help page (?add_dataframe), because it has
many arguments to pick the right columns. It still needs some testing,
but I think it will be more than ready for the next release (on May).
Any feedback would be very welcome.

Regards,
Iñaki

2018-03-12 20:26 GMT+01:00 Mark <slash...@gmail.com>:
> If I understand correctly, by default, simmer records data about different
> processes using a similar approach to the old "monitors" in SimPy.
> Is there an option to disable monitoring?

Yes, there is. Every resource, and every arrival source, has a "mon"
argument. If it's set to FALSE, that particular resource, or the
arrivals generated by that source, are not monitored.

> Also, SimPy had an alternative approach called "Tallies" that only kept a
> running aggregate value (such as mean, stdev, count) for the purpose of
> keeping memory consumption small.
> For very large, or very long-running simulations, what is the best way to
> only collect statistics on the metrics of interest?

The best way is to disable what you don't need. If it still does not
fit, you need to purchase more memory (or you have to rethink your
simulation ;-) ).

It's almost impossible to fit all the possible needs by implementing
some running summaries. And it's a burden to have to think about what
you have to collect and where. So the *simmer way* is to collect
everything automatically. Every decision has advantages and
shortcomings. This is *our* approach.

Nonetheless, there are some improvements to come. The implementation
of some kind of "connector" is on the roadmap, so that we will be able
to plug simmer's monitors to, e.g., files on disk or a SQL database.
But that's a medium-term goal.

I hope I have responded.

messages.body_plain:
Generically, it is possible to assign arrivals to a resource based upon a regularly-updated preference ranking of resources, then have the resource wait until it gets a batch?  To use the roller-coaster example, suppose there were five roller coasters and an "arrival" (amusement park rider) chooses between them based upon some preference order (e.g., a preference score based partially on the number of people currently waiting in the ride, and partially upon how far the person needs to walk, a defined value).

My use case is pretty specific, but I want to be able to assign arrivals to one of multiple discrete resources based upon a preference ranking.

Thanks
Ralph

2018-03-28 20:59 GMT+02:00 Ralph Asher <ralph....@gmail.com>:
> Generically, it is possible to assign arrivals to a resource based upon a
> regularly-updated preference ranking of resources, then have the resource
> wait until it gets a batch?  To use the roller-coaster example, suppose
> there were five roller coasters and an "arrival" (amusement park rider)
> chooses between them based upon some preference order (e.g., a preference
> score based partially on the number of people currently waiting in the ride,
> and partially upon how far the person needs to walk, a defined value).

A branch should do the trick. In the 'option' argument, you have
freedom to implement your decider function based on a rank or whatever
you need. Then, each subtrajectory contains a roller-coaster. What you
can't do, in principle, is to rely on queue counts for that decider,
because arrivals wait *in the batch*, not in the resource. You can
solve this by setting some global variables:

- batch option=potentially_complex_function_here,
  - trajectory1
    - set_global "resource1" +1
    - batch
    - set_global "resource1" 0
    - seize "resource1"
    - ...
  - trajectory2
    - set_global "resource2" +1
    - batch
    - set_global "resource2" 0
    - seize "resource2"
    - ...
  - ...

etcetera. Your globals effectively are your queue counters, and you
can check them in the branch decider.

Also note that, with the latest version, incrementing an attribute
(global or not) can be done simply as follows:

set_attribute("my_key", 1, mod="+")
set_global("my_key", 1, mod="+")

Iñaki

> My use case is pretty specific, but I want to be able to assign arrivals to
> one of multiple discrete resources based upon a preference ranking.
>
> Thanks
> Ralph

I'm not sure I understand. You can have a data frame listing all the
attributes, but you need to list all the sub-trajectories in either
case. If you are worried about the amount of code to write, given that
the sub-trajectories are equal except for the resource to
seize/release, you can parametrise them into a function and use lapply
to obtain a list of trajectories (see for instance how we build
'bh_traffic' in [1], and how we add a lot of resources further below
with a loop). Once you have all the sub-trajectories as a list, it is
easy to pass them to a branch using do.call.

> I'm thinking of how to make it flexible enough to
> support many (or few) roller-coasters without needing to explicitly list
> them all in the simmer object.

In general, see the techniques used in [1]. These simulations are able
to deal with a large number of resources and entities with similar
trajectories with the minimum number of lines of code, with a heavy
use of lapply and for loops to build such trajectories and simulation
environments.

BTW, as this is becoming a kind of recurring topic, I think that this
pattern may be a good candidate for simmer.bricks. I opened an issue
there [2] to consider this feature. Any feedback would be very
welcome. And if you are able to build this brick for your simulation,
it would be very welcome as a PR. ;-)

>>> > Generically, it is possible to assign arrivals to a resource based upon

>>> > regularly-updated preference ranking of resources, then have the
>>> > resource

>>> A branch should do the trick. In the 'option' argument, you have
>>> freedom to implement your decider function based on a rank or whatever
>>> you need. Then, each subtrajectory contains a roller-coaster. What you
>>> can't do, in principle, is to rely on queue counts for that decider,
>>> because arrivals wait *in the batch*, not in the resource. You can
>>> solve this by setting some global variables:
>>>
>>> - batch option=potentially_complex_function_here,
>>>   - trajectory1
>>>     - set_global "resource1" +1
>>>     - batch
>>>     - set_global "resource1" 0
>>>     - seize "resource1"
>>>     - ...
>>>   - trajectory2
>>>     - set_global "resource2" +1
>>>     - batch
>>>     - set_global "resource2" 0
>>>     - seize "resource2"
>>>     - ...
>>>   - ...
>>>
>>> etcetera. Your globals effectively are your queue counters, and you
>>> can check them in the branch decider.
>>>
>>> Also note that, with the latest version, incrementing an attribute
>>> (global or not) can be done simply as follows:
>>>
>>> set_attribute("my_key", 1, mod="+")
>>> set_global("my_key", 1, mod="+")
